opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think evolution is really the right frame because it's the one process that actually generated all of the biology we're trying to model. Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution, as the saying goes, and I think that's just as true for machine learning on biology as it is for biology itself.

When you train a model on DNA, RNA, or protein sequences across the tree of life, what you're really doing is learning from billions of years of experiments that nature has already run. Every sequence that exists today is a survivor: it's been tested against selection, so it carries information about what works, what's constrained, and what's tolerated. Conservation across species tells you what's functionally important. Variation tells you where there's flexibility. Co-variation between positions tells you about structure and interactions. A model trained at that scale can soak up all of that signal implicitly, without us having to hand-label function.

That's part of why we've been excited about working at the level of DNA, genomes and not just individual proteins. The central dogma means DNA is the foundational layer: it encodes the RNAs, the proteins, the regulatory logic, the way genes are organized into operons and pathways. If you model evolution at the genome scale, you can in principle capture all of those modalities and their interactions in one model, rather than building a separate model for every molecule type.

And I think it gives you a path from prediction to design. If a model has really internalized the rules evolution has explored, you can start asking it to generate new sequences that are plausible under those rules but that nature never actually sampled. Evolution only explored a tiny fraction of possible sequence space, because it's path-dependent and it's optimizing for fitness in a particular environment, not for what we might want, like a better gene editor or a new therapeutic. So the idea is to use evolution as the training signal and then go beyond it.

The open question, and what I find most interesting, is how far that scales. Does evolutionary data alone get you to models that understand cells and organisms, or do you need to bring in experimental perturbation data, things like single-cell measurements of what happens when you knock out genes, to close the loop between sequence and function? My bet is that you need both: evolution as the unifying prior, and lab experiments to ground it and push it in the directions we care about.

astra-6.text:
I think evolution gives us a framework for connecting biology across scales. We tend to study DNA, RNA, proteins, cells, and organisms as separate things, partly because we have different tools for measuring them. But they’re all connected through this process of variation and selection. A protein’s function depends on the cell it’s in, and the fitness of that cell depends on its environment.

So when we think about building biological models, the question is: can we learn those relationships, rather than just learn the patterns in each type of data independently? Every genome we sequence is the result of an evolutionary history. That gives us an enormous amount of information about which changes biology can tolerate and which combinations of changes work together.

But there’s an important limitation: evolution gives us the outcomes of experiments, without a complete record of the conditions under which those experiments happened. Sequence data alone doesn’t tell you everything about function or fitness. You need to connect it to experiments where you perturb a system and measure what happens.

To me, that’s the opportunity: use evolution to organize what we learn from biological diversity, then use experiments to make those models predictive. Can we predict what happens when we introduce a mutation, change an environment, or build a sequence that evolution hasn’t explored? That’s a much deeper test than whether a model can generate something that looks biological.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evolution gives us a common framework for understanding why biology looks the way it does. A protein, a cell, or an organism isn’t designed in isolation. It’s the product of variation and selection, operating under physical constraints and in a particular environment.

That’s useful for building models because the diversity of life contains information about what works. When you compare related sequences, you can see which features are conserved, which can change, and which changes tend to occur together. Those patterns can help us learn constraints that would be difficult to discover from individual experiments alone.

But evolution also gives us a way to connect scales. Changes in DNA affect molecular function, which affects cells, which ultimately affects reproductive success in an environment. Ideally, a biological model would connect those levels rather than just recognize patterns within one of them.

The caveat is that evolution doesn’t optimize a single, universal objective. There’s historical contingency, drift, and changing environments. So I’d treat it as a unifying framework for asking questions and constraining models, rather than a complete explanation by itself.
